questions.q: Why should data quality checks run against staged data rather than after data has already reached the warehouse?
options: Catching a problem in staging costs a re-run of one load; catching it after it's already in the warehouse can mean a wrong number in a live report
The warehouse is physically incapable of storing invalid data
Data quality checks are only possible using SSIS, never plain SQL
Staging tables automatically reject bad data without any explicit checks
questions.explain: Staging is a safe place to fail (Lesson 21) — validating there, before a load into fact or dimension tables, keeps bad data from ever reaching something analysts are actively querying.

questions.q: What does a referential integrity check in staging confirm?
options: That a fact row's dimension key actually exists in the corresponding dimension table before that row loads
That every column in the staging table has a unique value
That the staging table's file size hasn't changed since the last load
That the source system's password is still valid
questions.explain: Without this check, a fact row referencing a dimension key the dimension has never heard of can silently produce nulls or dropped rows deep inside the warehouse.

questions.q: Why does an undetected duplicate row matter for a fact table?
options: It inflates every additive measure that touches it, such as double-counting revenue
It has no effect at all on any warehouse query
It automatically triggers a full warehouse rebuild
It only affects dimension tables, never fact tables
questions.explain: The same source row landing twice — from a re-run or a duplicate upstream event — inflates any SUM or COUNT that includes it unless a staging-level duplicate check catches it first.

questions.q: What is the one thing you should never do with a row that fails a data quality check?
options: Quietly drop it with no record anywhere that it happened
Reject it and log the reason in a quarantine table
Substitute a known 'Unknown' placeholder and flag the row
Stop the entire batch if the failure is severe enough
questions.explain: Silently dropping a row with no trace turns a real data problem into an untraceable mystery later — some form of logging or counting is essential, whichever handling policy is chosen.

questions.q: Why is a type/format mismatch check still needed even though staging columns are loosely typed on purpose (Lesson 22)?
options: A malformed value not failing the load still needs to fail somewhere before it reaches a strictly typed warehouse column
Loosely typed columns automatically convert any value to the correct type
Type mismatches can only occur in the warehouse, never in staging
Loose typing means quality checks are unnecessary entirely
questions.explain: Loosely typed staging columns exist precisely so a bad value doesn't fail the extract — but that value must still be caught by an explicit check before it's asked to become, say, a DATE or an INT in the warehouse.
